newsitem.title: UK: Bundesbank caps dollar but rally not over yet -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank caps dollar but rally not over yet -analysts.

text.p: The dollar romped to 34-month highs against the mark in Europe on Wednesday, only to skid when the Bundesbank insisted it did not believe the bullish currency should climb any further.

A news agency report that Germany would welcome further dollar strength boosted the U.S. unit overnight, but the Bundesbank said it continued to support the view, recently expressed by the Group of Seven industrialised nations, that the dollar had already corrected.
Analysts said the Bundesbank had probably capped the dollar for Wednesday but believed the rally still had further to run.
"I think we've seen the highs for the day, but I doubt we've even seen the highs for the week," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at Union Bank of Switzerland.
The dollar was at 1.6823 marks at early afternoon, off a session low of 1.6745 but well below the 1.6935 peak it scaled in early trade, its highest level since April 1994.
It slipped to 123.80 yen from its high of 124.48. Both rates were still above late Tuesday's European levels of 1.6720 marks and 122.80 yen.
Analysts said the response to the Bundesbank statement was symptomatic of a market on tenterhooks for intervention.
"Whenever you see a big move there's going to be sensitivity but it's just a case of wait and see," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
The dollar has gained more than 15 percent against the mark -- 10 percent of that in this year alone -- and 17 percent against the yen since its bull run began last August.
Analysts felt concerted intervention at current levels was unlikely, but did not rule out unilateral Japanese action.
"Very near-term it could be that the Japanese finally lose patience and decide to do something themselves," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi.
Japan's Ministry of Finance fuelled such fears on Wednesday, saying Japan would "take appropriate measures to tackle any excessive moves" in the forex markets.

Economists said the beneficial effects of yen weakness were wearing off and rising import costs were dampening the profitability of other sectors of the economy. Germany and the United States had little interest in selling dollars, they said.

U.S. January retail sales and producer price data due out on Thursday and Friday should exacerbate the woes of the yen and, in particular, the mark as they highlight the health of the U.S. economy compared with those of its G3 fellows, analysts said.

"The (German) labour market, the increasingly tight fiscal policy and the very loose monetary policy with bund yields hitting post-war lows yesterday are all profoundly negative for the deutschemark," said UBS's von Maydell.
In its statement, the Bundesbank said it still backed the view that currency "misalignments" had been corrected, as the G7 stated last weekend after its meeting in Berlin.
"The statement said the dollar has been corrected, and it was made at a rate of 1.65 marks," said chief Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber.
News agency MNSI had quoted German officials as saying they would welcome a dollar rise to a range of 1.70 to 1.75 marks.
